props.title: Bent

sections.content: **Bent** (1997) stands as one of cinema's most powerful depictions of LGBTQ+ persecution during the Holocaust, based on Martin Sherman's groundbreaking 1979 play. Clive Owen delivers a haunting performance as Max, a gay man in 1930s Berlin who witnesses the brutality of the Nazi regime firsthand. The film builds on earlier Holocaust cinema like **Schindler's List** (1993) but specifically highlights the often-overlooked persecution of gay men, marked by the pink triangle. Director Sean Mathias crafts devastating scenes of intimacy amid horror, particularly in the stone-carrying sequences between Max and Horst (Lothaire Bluteau).

sections.content: The film's Berlin sequences, featuring Mick Jagger as drag performer Greta, capture the decadent nightlife of the Weimar Republic that was violently suppressed by the Nazi regime. This period was similarly depicted in **Cabaret** (1972), though **Bent** takes a darker turn in showing the systematic destruction of this liberal culture. The film's stark concentration camp scenes influenced later LGBTQ+ historical dramas like **Milk** (2008) and **The Danish Girl** (2015), proving that powerful stories of persecution and resistance needed to be told.

What sets **Bent** apart is its unflinching portrayal of love surviving in the most inhuman conditions. The central relationship between Max and Horst develops through spoken intimacy alone - they cannot touch or look at each other while working. This innovative dramatic device influenced later films like **The Way He Looks** (2014) and **Portrait of a Lady on Fire** (2019) in depicting forbidden love through restraint and suggestion rather than physical contact. sections.content: **Bent** helped pave the way for more diverse Holocaust narratives, influencing films like **Aimée & Jaguar** (1999) and **Phoenix** (2014) that explore different perspectives on Nazi persecution. The film's success also contributed to broader acceptance of LGBTQ+ historical dramas, leading to works like **Pride** (2014) and **BPM (Beats Per Minute)** (2017) that connect past struggles to contemporary LGBTQ+ rights movements.
